maya: Quick sanity check — bringing up a new compact embed: `stork-compact-int4` on the MINI-QA holdout. Initial numbers look a bit off at k=1.
maya: Baseline `heron-embed` (fp16) recall@1/5/10 = 0.662 / 0.805 / 0.873
maya: `stork-compact-int4` (our quantized build) recall@1/5/10 = 0.619 / 0.781 / 0.842
maya: That's ~4.3pt drop at R@1. Data/pipe kept constant (same tokenizer, same precompute). Anyone seen this pattern with int4 or compact models before? :thinking_face:
andre: Can you paste the eval command and the holdout size? Also confirm L2 norm vs cosine handling — mismatch there often kills R@1.
maya: Eval command:
```
python eval_recall.py --model stork-compact-int4 --holdout miniqa_holdout_v2.jsonl --metric recall --ks 1,5,10 --normalize True --batch 512
```
maya: Holdout size = 12,000 queries (balanced by answer length). I used `--normalize True` for both model outputs.
liam: Two quick checks: 1) verify the nearest neighbor distance distribution vs baseline, 2) check short-answer (<32 tokens) vs long-answer bins. quantization sometimes compresses high-similarity mass.
sara: Also check whether we applied the same whitening/pca step (if any). I remember we had an accidental whitening toggle in the v2 eval script.
maya: Good point — I explicitly disabled PCA. No whitening on either run. I can dump the top-10 distances.
maya: Top-10 dist histogram (euclidean) — baseline mean top1=0.128, stork mean top1=0.163; stork distances are shifted right.
andre: That shift suggests scaling or clamping from quantization. Did you use per-channel quant or per-tensor? int4 per-tensor usually blurs peaks.
maya: This build used per-tensor symmetric quant + clamp. I can try per-channel asymmetric and re-run.
liam: Also try running a small subset with fp16 stork (unquantized) to see if architecture itself has a small drop vs heron. If fp16 stork matches heron, it's quant-related.
maya: OK queued run: `stork-fp16` on same holdout (quick 2k subset first). Will post numbers when done.

eval-bot: [run 2233445566-1] eval_recall.py finished: model=stork-fp16 subset=2k recall@1/5/10 = 0.658 / 0.799 / 0.869
maya: fp16 stork is almost parity with heron (within noise). So architecture likely fine — quant is the culprit.
sara: Next try: per-channel int4 + scale calibration with a heldout calibration set (not the same holdout). Also test L2 vs no-L2 if distances change distribution.
andre: Can you produce nearest-neighbor agreement metric: fraction where top1 index is identical between baseline and candidate? If recall drop but top1 overlap is high, might be reordering noise.
maya: Overlap baseline->stork-int4 top1 = 0.74 (so 26% mismatch). Baseline->stork-fp16 overlap = 0.91. So quantization introduces ~17% permute.
liam: That's big. Try per-channel and a slightly higher clipping percentile (e.g., 99.9 -> 99.99) during calibration.
maya: I'll re-run per-channel asymmetric + clip 99.99. Also doing per-length bins to make sure short answers aren't disproportionately impacted.

maya: quick note — latency/size looks good: stork-int4 mean embed latency 3.2ms vs heron-fp16 8.1ms. So big win if we can recover R@1.
andre: Nice. Make sure we log per-query failure cases — dump examples where baseline top1 != candidate top1 and examine semantic gap.
maya: Will do. Plan: rerun per-channel asymmetric int4 + clip99.99, log 200 mismatch examples, run per-length bins, then report.
liam: Sounds good. If per-channel doesn't help, consider int6 experiment or hybrid (fp16 head + int4 body).
maya: OK I'll kick off the runs now. Will update in this thread with results. Thanks all :thumbsup:
